source_text: Nos vero nihil habemus, quod in nostro admirandum credamus ingenio, quia intellegimus nec peccatum sine voluntate, nec sine Deo corpora, nec sine corporibus sensus corporum, nec sine commixtione coniugia, nec sine Deo operatore existere posse nascentes; et indubitatum tenemus, neque divinum esse, quod doceatur iniustum; neque quod divinum sit, posse iniustum doceri. Non minus autem, quam ea quae diximus, relucet esse iniquum, si aliorum peccata aliis, qui ibi nec fuerint, nedum consenserint, imputentur. Proinde his illuminati solibus iure optimo Manichaeorum antra despicimus, qui putant vel esse posse sine voluntate peccatum, vel non a Deo homines fieri, vel ad alium auctorem sensum corporum, et ad alium corpora pertinere; vel Deum esse, qui iniquitatum criminibus opprimatur; aut scelere iniquitatis urgeri eum, qui aeternus omnium conditor aestimetur; aut umbram aliquam tenere iustitiae, si aliorum voluntates aliorum applicentur exortibus. Ac per hoc merita partium negotiis, non ingeniis imputamus.
pass_a_gloss: But we have nothing that we believe admirable in our talent, because we understand that neither sin without will, nor bodies without God, nor senses of bodies without bodies, nor marriages without mingling, nor those being born without God as worker can exist; and we hold it undoubted that neither is that divine which is taught unjust; nor can that which is divine be taught unjust. No less however than those things which we have said, it shines that it is inequitable if the sins of others are imputed to others who were not even there, still less consented. Accordingly, illuminated by these suns, by best right we despise the caves of the Manichaeans, who think either that there can be sin without will, or that humans are not made by God, or that the sense of bodies belongs to one author and bodies to another; or that he is God who is oppressed by charges of iniquities; or that he is pressed by the crime of iniquity who is estimated the eternal founder of all; or that any shadow of justice is held if the wills of some are applied to the origins of others. And through this we impute the deserts of the parties to the businesses, not to talents.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: I, however, find nothing to admire in my own talent because I understand that sin cannot exist without will, bodies without God, bodily sensations without bodies, marriage without union, or newborn people without God’s activity. And I hold as certain that what is proved unjust is not divine, and what is divine cannot be proved unjust. It is no less plain than these things that imputing one person’s sins to others who were not even there, much less consenting, is unjust. Enlightened by these suns, I am entirely justified in looking down on the Manichaeans’ caves. They think either that sin can exist without will, or that God does not make human beings, or that bodily sensation belongs to one author and bodies to another. They suppose either that someone weighed down by charges of injustice is God, or that the eternal creator of all can be charged with the crime of injustice, or that even a shadow of justice remains when one person’s acts of will are attached to another person’s birth. Accordingly, I assess the merits of the opposing sides by their causes, not by their talents.

choices.why: Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
